patient.name: Theo Mensah
patient.setting: GP surgery, then Paediatric Emergency Department the next day
patient.complaint: Swollen, red left eyelid after a week-long cold, then double vision
background: Blocked nose and cold for 7 days
Otherwise healthy; vaccinations up to date
Lives with his mum and sister in Walthamstow

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a child with a red swollen eyelid after sinusitis: proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, diplopia or reduced vision mean orbital, not periorbital, cellulitis.

points: Day 1, GP: Theo's **left upper eyelid** is red, swollen and tender.
He has a mild fever after a week of blocked nose.
He can open the eye; vision is normal.
Eye movements full and painless; **no proptosis**.

steps.lead: On day 1 Theo's infection is in the eyelid skin, **in front of the orbital septum**: periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis, after a cold.
Theo is a **child**, the group most affected by both forms.
Day 1 fits **periorbital**: swollen tender lid and fever, but vision, pupils and movements are **normal** with **no proptosis**.

points: Day 2: Theo **cannot open** the left eye; he is drowsy and hot.
He sees **double** and it hurts to look up.
The left eye is **pushed forward**; the conjunctiva is swollen.

steps.q: Theo now has proptosis, painful restricted eye movements and diplopia. Which is the diagnosis?
steps.r: Any change in **vision, eye movement or proptosis** means the infection is **behind the septum**: orbital cellulitis, an emergency.

steps.lead: Theo has many **red flags**: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, reduced acuity, chemosis, reduced eye opening, fever and systemic illness.

visual.title: Theo's proptosis (left minus right, Hertel)
visual.label: Theo 4 mm
visual.caption: The left eye sits 4 mm further forward: something is filling the orbit behind the septum.

steps.title: Periorbital vs orbital cellulitis
head: Feature
Periorbital (preseptal)
Orbital (postseptal)
rows: Lid and skin in front of septum
Oral antibiotics if mild and well

steps.lead: Untreated, Theo risks **vision loss**, an **orbital abscess**, **cavernous sinus thrombosis** and meningitis.

steps.text: A very swollen lid does not make it orbital. Only **proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, reduced acuity or RAPD** do. Always force the lids open and check.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' with the answer contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain, alongside urgent ophthalmology and ENT review.

steps.lead: Theo's red flags mean **urgent ophthalmology and ENT review** and bloods now.

steps.title: Theo's bloods
steps.text: A marked neutrophilia and high CRP: a serious bacterial infection. Cultures before IV antibiotics.

visual.title: Theo's CRP
visual.label: Theo 148
visual.caption: A useful baseline to track his response to IV antibiotics.

o: Contrast-enhanced CT of orbits, sinuses and brain
steps.r: **Contrast-enhanced CT** of orbits, sinuses and brain shows the extent, any **abscess** and intracranial spread.

steps.lead: Theo's diagnosis is **clinical plus urgent CT**: it shows **left ethmoid sinusitis** with a small medial subperiosteal collection.

steps.text: Image when orbital cellulitis is suspected: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, reduced acuity, or no improvement on antibiotics. The answer is **CT with contrast**, not plain films.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' with mild periorbital cellulitis in a well child (oral co-amoxiclav, safety-net) versus orbital cellulitis (admit, IV cefotaxime or clindamycin, urgent ophthalmology and ENT).

steps.lead: On day 1 Theo was mild and well: **oral co-amoxiclav**, close follow-up and a clear **safety-net** to return if his eye changed.

steps.q: Theo is back on day 2 with proptosis and diplopia. What now?
o: Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
steps.r: Orbital cellulitis needs **admission and IV antibiotics** with urgent ophthalmology and ENT review.

steps.lead: Theo is **admitted** for **IV cefotaxime**, with urgent ophthalmology and ENT review, ready for **surgical drainage** if needed.

steps.title: Red swollen eyelid: what to do
nodes: Check vision, pupils, eye movements, proptosis
All normal, well → periorbital: oral co-amoxiclav, safety-net
Any abnormal → orbital: admit, IV antibiotics
Urgent CT with contrast; ophthalmology + ENT
Abscess or worsening vision → surgical drainage
steps.caption: The eye examination decides the pathway.

visual.title: Theo's response to IV cefotaxime
visual.caption: Fever and CRP settle; his small collection resolves without surgery.

steps.text: Do not send home on oral antibiotics once there is proptosis or ophthalmoplegia. IV antibiotics are needed because of the risk of **cavernous sinus thrombosis** and intracranial spread.
Children with periorbital cellulitis who are unwell or very young get **IV antibiotics** too. Safety-net everyone for orbital progression.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the commonest organisms and source, why the orbital septum separates the two conditions, and why orbital infection reaches the cavernous sinus.

steps.lead: Theo's infection spread **contiguously** from his **ethmoid sinus**; **S. pneumoniae** often travels this way in children.

steps.q: Which sinus most often seeds orbital cellulitis in children like Theo?
steps.r: The **ethmoid** sinus is separated from the orbit by the paper-thin **lamina papyracea**, so infection crosses easily.

steps.lead: On day 1 Theo's **orbital septum** held the infection in front; by day 2 it had reached behind, threatening globe, muscles and apex.

steps.title: From cold to cavernous sinus
nodes: Spread through thin medial orbital wall
Valveless orbital veins → cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis

steps.lead: Theo's diplopia came from **muscle restriction**; his reduced acuity warns of **compressive optic neuropathy**; valveless veins risk **cavernous sinus thrombosis**.

steps.text: Cavernous sinus thrombosis clues: **bilateral** eye signs, CN III, IV and VI palsies, V1/V2 numbness, severe headache and a very unwell patient.

mcq.q: Which structure separates periorbital from orbital cellulitis?
mcq.r: The **orbital septum**: periorbital is anterior, orbital is posterior.

mcq.q: Which finding indicates orbital rather than periorbital cellulitis?
mcq.r: **Proptosis** (or painful restricted movement, reduced acuity) means postseptal infection.

mcq.q: Which age group is most affected by periorbital and orbital cellulitis?
Which is a serious intracranial complication of orbital cellulitis?
mcq.r: **Cavernous sinus thrombosis**, via valveless orbital veins.

mcq.q: Which is the best imaging for suspected orbital cellulitis?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of orbits, sinuses and brain
mcq.r: **Contrast CT** of orbits, sinuses and brain.

mcq.q: What is first-line for mild periorbital cellulitis in a well patient?
mcq.r: **Oral co-amoxiclav** with close follow-up and safety-netting.

mcq.q: Which IV antibiotic is an example for orbital cellulitis in the notes?
Which specialties should urgently review orbital cellulitis?
Which organism often causes orbital cellulitis via ethmoid sinusitis in children?
mcq.r: **S. pneumoniae**; S. aureus and S. pyogenes are also common.

mcq.q: Why can orbital infection spread to the cavernous sinus?
o: The septum drains into the sinus

prompts.q: Define periorbital and orbital cellulitis, and name the common causes.

Orbital (postseptal): posterior to the septum; ophthalmological emergency

More common in children; orbital bone fracture predisposes

points.p: Vision, pupils and eye movements normal

points.p: Vision loss

points.p: Meningitis and intracranial spread

Urgent ophthalmology and ENT review
Blood tests (FBC, CRP, cultures)

IV antibiotics if paediatric concern or more significant infection
Safety-net and review for orbital progression

IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, e.g. cefotaxime or clindamycin
Urgent ophthalmology and ENT review
Surgical drainage if needed

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: contiguous spread from the sinuses.

points.p: Contiguous spread from paranasal sinus, skin infection, insect bite, trauma
S. aureus
S. pyogenes
S. pneumoniae, often via ethmoid sinusitis in children

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: barrier, then pressure, then veins.

points.p: Septum separates preseptal and postseptal compartments
points.why: Its integrity decides if globe, muscles and apex are at risk.

Extraocular muscle restriction: ophthalmoplegia, diplopia

glossary.periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the eyelid and skin in front of the orbital septum; also called preseptal cellulitis.
glossary.preseptal cellulitis: Another name for periorbital cellulitis: infection anterior to the orbital septum.
glossary.orbital cellulitis: Infection behind the orbital septum involving orbital fat and muscles; an emergency.
glossary.postseptal: Behind the orbital septum, inside the orbit.
glossary.orbital septum: Thin fibrous sheet from the orbital rim to the eyelids that walls off the orbit.
glossary.orbit: The bony eye socket, made of seven bones.
glossary.proptosis: Forward bulging of the eye, caused by something filling the orbit.
glossary.exophthalmos: Protrusion of the eye; often used for thyroid eye disease.
glossary.Hertel exophthalmometer: Instrument that measures how far each eye protrudes.
glossary.ophthalmoplegia: Weakness or restriction of eye movements.
glossary.conjunctiva: Thin membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids.
glossary.RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: a sign of optic nerve damage on the swinging light test.
glossary.visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart.
glossary.compressive optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from pressure, causing reduced acuity, colour loss and RAPD.
glossary.orbital apex: Back of the orbit where the optic nerve and eye-movement nerves enter.
glossary.subperiosteal abscess: Collection of pus between the orbital bone and its periosteum, usually next to the ethmoid sinus.
glossary.cavernous sinus thrombosis: Infected clot in the venous sinus beside the pituitary, causing bilateral eye signs and cranial nerve palsies.
glossary.cavernous sinus: Venous channel beside the pituitary containing CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI and the carotid artery.
glossary.valveless veins: Orbital veins with no valves, so blood and infection can flow back to the cavernous sinus.
glossary.meningitis: Infection and inflammation of the membranes around the brain.
glossary.paranasal sinuses: Air spaces around the nose: frontal, ethmoid, maxillary and sphenoid.
glossary.ethmoid sinus: Sinus between the eyes, separated from the orbit by a very thin bone wall.
glossary.lamina papyracea: Paper-thin medial orbital wall over the ethmoid sinus; infection crosses it easily.
glossary.sinusitis: Infection or inflammation of the paranasal sinuses.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, e.g. a cold.
glossary.S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive coccus causing skin and soft tissue infection.
glossary.S. pyogenes: Group A streptococcus: a common cause of cellulitis.
glossary.S. pneumoniae: Pneumococcus: a common sinus pathogen that can spread to the orbit.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; oral first-line for mild periorbital cellulitis.
glossary.cefotaxime: IV third-generation cephalosporin used for orbital cellulitis.
glossary.clindamycin: Antibiotic active against staph, strep and anaerobes; an IV option for orbital cellulitis.
glossary.ENT: Ear, nose and throat surgery; treats and drains the sinus source.
glossary.safety-net: Clear advice on which changes mean coming back urgently.
glossary.dacryocystitis: Infection of the tear sac, causing a red swelling at the inner corner of the eye.
glossary.thyroid eye disease: Autoimmune orbital inflammation in Graves' disease causing proptosis and lid retraction.
glossary.retrobulbar haemorrhage: Bleeding behind the eye after trauma, causing sudden proptosis and visual loss.

technique.stem: A 6 year old girl has a 2 day history of a swollen, red right upper eyelid following a cold. Today she complains that it hurts to move her right eye and she is seeing double. Her temperature is 39.0°C and pulse rate 136 bpm. The right eye is pushed forward and movements are restricted in all directions.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a red swollen eyelid: decide preseptal or postseptal.

clues: hurts to move her right eye
steps.x: URTI source, **painful ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, proptosis**, fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Eye involvement means behind the septum: **orbital cellulitis**.

elim: Allergic conjunctivitis is itchy and bilateral with no proptosis or fever.
Dacryocystitis is a swelling at the medial canthus over the tear sac.
Periorbital cellulitis has normal eye movements and no proptosis.
Thyroid eye disease is painless, slow and not febrile; rare in children.

steps.x: **C. Orbital cellulitis.** Proptosis or ophthalmoplegia = postseptal = emergency.

technique.stem: A 10 year old boy has a 3 day history of left eyelid swelling after sinusitis. He has left proptosis, painful eye movements and left visual acuity of 6/18. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. IV antibiotics have been started.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain
Non-contrast CT of the head only

steps.x: Imaging for suspected orbital cellulitis.
Orbital cellulitis with reduced vision: look for an **abscess** and intracranial spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Contrast-enhanced CT of orbits, sinuses and brain**.

elim: The spine is irrelevant.
Without contrast and without orbits and sinuses, an abscess may be missed.
Ultrasound cannot assess the sinuses or brain.
Plain films do not show orbital collections.

steps.x: **A. Contrast CT of orbits, sinuses and brain.**

technique.stem: A 7 year old boy has a red, swollen left eyelid and fever after a week of nasal congestion. He has left proptosis and diplopia on looking to the left. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Admit for IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with urgent ophthalmology and ENT review
Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 48 hours
Urgent outpatient ophthalmology clinic next week

steps.x: Initial management: decide oral or IV, home or hospital.
Proptosis and diplopia: **orbital** cellulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Admit, IV antibiotics** (cefotaxime or clindamycin), urgent ophthalmology and ENT.

elim: Oral treatment is for mild periorbital cellulitis in a well child.
Oral treatment at home risks cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Topical antibiotics do not reach the orbit.
This is an emergency, not a clinic referral.

steps.x: **A. Admit for IV antibiotics.** Orbital = admit, IV, ophthalmology + ENT.

technique.stem: A 5 year old boy has a red, swollen right eyelid that developed after an insect bite 2 days ago. He is afebrile and playing normally. Visual acuity is normal, pupils react normally, eye movements are full and painless and there is no proptosis.
technique.q: Which anatomical structure best explains why his eye movements and vision are unaffected?

steps.x: Anatomy: what keeps periorbital infection out of the orbit?

clues: eye movements are full and painless
steps.x: Preseptal infection from a skin breach; orbit untouched.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **orbital septum** is the barrier.

elim: The lacrimal gland makes tears; it is not a barrier.
The lamina papyracea is the thin wall that lets sinus infection IN.
The tarsal plate stiffens the lid but does not wall off the orbit.
Tenon's capsule wraps the globe, not the septal plane.

steps.x: **C. Orbital septum.** Anterior = periorbital; posterior = orbital.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy has had a blocked nose for a week. For 2 days his left eye has been swollen and red, and today he has double vision and pain when looking up. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. The left eye is proptosed with chemosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sinusitis followed by proptosis, chemosis, painful eye movement and diplopia with fever is orbital cellulitis. Periorbital cellulitis spares vision, movements and position of the eye.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a red swollen eye in a child.

clues: double vision and pain when looking up
steps.x: Sinus source, **diplopia, painful movement, proptosis, chemosis**, fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Orbital cellulitis**.

elim: Dacryocystitis is a medial canthal swelling without proptosis.
Allergy is itchy and afebrile.
Periorbital cellulitis has normal eye movements and no proptosis.
Thyroid eye disease is painless and slow, without fever.

steps.x: **C. Orbital cellulitis.** Red flags = postseptal.

practice.stem: A 4 year old girl has a red, swollen, tender left upper eyelid 1 day after a mosquito bite on the lid. She is eating and playing normally. Her temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 110 bpm. Vision is normal for age, pupils are normal, eye movements are full and painless and there is no proptosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A red, tender lid after a skin breach with normal vision, pupils and movements and no proptosis is periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis. Orbital cellulitis would affect movements or eye position.

steps.x: Preseptal or postseptal?

clues: eye movements are full and painless
steps.x: Skin source, systemically well, eye examination **normal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis**.

elim: Cavernous sinus thrombosis gives bilateral signs and a very unwell child.
A chalazion is a painless lid lump without diffuse redness.
Orbital cellulitis affects movement, vision or eye position.
An abscess causes proptosis and restricted movement.

steps.x: **D. Periorbital cellulitis.** Normal eye exam = preseptal.

practice.stem: A 7 year old boy has had a red, swollen right eyelid for 24 hours after a cold. The GP is deciding whether this is periorbital or orbital cellulitis. His temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 112 bpm.
practice.q: Which finding would most strongly suggest orbital cellulitis?
practice.e: Painful, restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia) mean the infection is behind the septum. Lid redness, tenderness, fever and a preceding URTI occur in both forms.

steps.x: Which single sign separates orbital from periorbital?
You need a sign that only postseptal infection causes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Painful, restricted eye movements** (or proptosis, reduced acuity).

elim: Erythema is present in both.
Tenderness is present in both.
Fever occurs in both.
A URTI precedes both.

steps.x: **D. Painful, restricted eye movements.**

practice.stem: A 12 year old girl is being treated with IV antibiotics for right orbital cellulitis. On day 2 she develops a severe headache and vomiting, and the left eye becomes swollen and proptosed. There is bilateral ophthalmoplegia and reduced sensation over the forehead. Her temperature is 39.8°C, pulse rate 140 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Spread to the opposite eye, bilateral ophthalmoplegia, V1 numbness and severe headache mean spread via valveless orbital veins to the cavernous sinus. A subperiosteal abscess stays on one side.

steps.x: A complication of orbital cellulitis.

clues: the left eye becomes swollen and proptosed
steps.x: Spread to the **other eye**, cranial nerves III, IV, VI and **V1**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cavernous sinus thrombosis**.

elim: Meningitis does not cause bilateral proptosis and V1 loss.
CRAO is painless sudden visual loss in one eye.
An abscess is unilateral.
Thyroid eye disease is not acute or febrile.

steps.x: **B. Cavernous sinus thrombosis.** Bilateral signs + cranial nerves = cavernous sinus.

practice.stem: A 6 year old boy has orbital cellulitis following acute ethmoid sinusitis. He has had no skin injury or insect bite. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive diplococci.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: S. pneumoniae, a Gram-positive diplococcus, often reaches the orbit via ethmoid sinusitis in children. Neisseria are Gram-negative diplococci; E. coli and Pseudomonas are Gram-negative rods.

steps.x: Organism question: use the source and the Gram stain.
Sinus source in a child, Gram-positive diplococci.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**.

elim: Chlamydia causes conjunctivitis and does not Gram stain.
E. coli is a Gram-negative rod.
Neisseria are Gram-negative diplococci causing hyperacute conjunctivitis.
Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod linked to contact lenses.

steps.x: **E. S. pneumoniae.** Ethmoid sinusitis in a child, Gram-positive diplococci.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man sustained a left zygomatic fracture in an assault 6 days ago. He now has increasing pain and swelling around the left eye, fever and double vision. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. The left eye is proptosed with chemosis and restricted movements.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Orbital bone fracture predisposes to orbital cellulitis; fever, raised inflammatory markers, proptosis, chemosis and ophthalmoplegia days later confirm it. Retrobulbar haemorrhage occurs immediately after injury without fever.

steps.x: Diagnosis after facial trauma.

clues: proptosed with chemosis and restricted movements
steps.x: Orbital bone fracture, days later fever, proptosis and ophthalmoplegia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Orbital cellulitis**.

elim: A fistula gives a pulsatile eye and bruit, not fever.
Periorbital cellulitis has normal eye movements and no proptosis.
Retrobulbar haemorrhage is immediate, afebrile, after injury.
Thyroid eye disease is not febrile or post-traumatic.

steps.x: **B. Orbital cellulitis.** Orbital fractures predispose to it.

practice.stem: A 13 year old girl has right proptosis, painful restricted eye movements and fever 2 days after sinusitis. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. She has been admitted and started on IV cefotaxime.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain
Non-contrast CT of the head only
practice.e: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain is the best imaging: it shows the sinus source, any abscess and intracranial spread. Plain films and ultrasound are inadequate.

steps.x: Imaging for orbital cellulitis.
Confirmed orbital red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Contrast CT of orbits, sinuses and brain**.

elim: The lumbar spine is irrelevant.
Head only and without contrast misses orbital and sinus disease.
Ultrasound cannot show sinuses or brain.
Plain films miss collections.

steps.x: **A. Contrast-enhanced CT.**

practice.stem: An 11 year old boy with left orbital cellulitis after ethmoid sinusitis has worsening proptosis despite 24 hours of IV antibiotics. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT?
o: Enlarged extraocular muscles with tendon sparing
Subperiosteal abscess next to an opacified ethmoid sinus
practice.e: Worsening proptosis despite IV antibiotics after ethmoid sinusitis suggests a medial subperiosteal abscess, a complication that may need drainage. Tendon-sparing muscle enlargement is thyroid eye disease.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' on CT in non-resolving orbital cellulitis.

clues: worsening proptosis despite 24 hours of IV antibiotics
steps.x: Sinus source and failure to respond: think **abscess**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subperiosteal abscess** beside the ethmoid sinus.

elim: Tendon-sparing muscle enlargement is thyroid eye disease.
There is no trauma.
Worsening proptosis means CT will not be normal.
A glioma is slow and painless.

steps.x: **E. Subperiosteal abscess.** Not improving on IV antibiotics: image and consider drainage.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy has a red, swollen right lower eyelid after scratching a spot 2 days ago. He is well and eating normally. His temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. Vision, pupils and eye movements are normal and there is no proptosis.

clues: He is well and eating normally
steps.x: Mild **periorbital** cellulitis in a well child.

elim: IV is for orbital cellulitis or a significant infection.
Nothing to drain.

Topical treatment does not treat cellulitis.

practice.stem: A 10 year old girl has a swollen left eye after a week of sinusitis. She has left proptosis and diplopia. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. She has no drug allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Admit for IV cefotaxime with urgent ophthalmology and ENT review
Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 48 hours
practice.e: Orbital cellulitis needs admission, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics such as cefotaxime and urgent ophthalmology and ENT review, because of the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

steps.x: Initial management of a red flag eye.
**Orbital** cellulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Oral treatment at home is unsafe in orbital disease.

practice.stem: A 12 year old boy with right orbital cellulitis has been on IV cefotaxime for 36 hours. His right visual acuity has fallen from 6/9 to 6/36 and a new right relative afferent pupillary defect has appeared. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 106/68 mmHg. CT shows a large medial subperiosteal abscess.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue IV cefotaxime and repeat CT in 1 week
Urgent surgical drainage of the abscess
practice.e: Falling acuity and a new RAPD mean compressive optic neuropathy from the abscess; urgent surgical drainage by ophthalmology and ENT is needed alongside IV antibiotics.

steps.x: Next step when orbital cellulitis worsens on IV antibiotics.

clues: new right relative afferent pupillary defect
steps.x: Sight is failing: **compressive optic neuropathy** from an abscess.

practice.stem: An 8 year old girl with left orbital cellulitis develops bilateral proptosis, bilateral ophthalmoplegia and severe headache. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 138 bpm and BP 94/56 mmHg. MRI venography shows thrombosis of the cavernous sinus.
practice.q: Which is the most likely route by which the infection reached the cavernous sinus?
o: Direct spread through the optic canal along the optic nerve
Haematogenous spread via the internal carotid artery
Lymphatic drainage to the cavernous sinus
Retrograde spread through valveless orbital veins
practice.e: The ophthalmic veins drain the orbit into the cavernous sinus and have no valves, so infected thrombus spreads backwards. The orbit has no significant lymphatic route to the sinus.

steps.x: Mechanism of intracranial spread.
Orbital infection, then venous sinus clot affecting both sides.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Valveless orbital (ophthalmic) veins**.

elim: The optic nerve is not the route to the cavernous sinus.
Arterial spread would not cause venous sinus thrombosis.
The orbit has no lymphatic route to the sinus.
The lacrimal duct drains into the nose, away from the sinus.

steps.x: **D. Valveless orbital veins.** The reason orbital cellulitis needs IV antibiotics.
